items.item: hot_standby_feedback prevents VACUUM from removing recently-dead rows a standby query might need, delaying cleanup on the primary instead

at.step: Reveal: a replica moves the cost, it does not remove it

items.item: A parallel JDBC read's bounds set a fixed-width stride across the key range; they never filter which rows are read, so every row still lands in some partition.

at.step: Reveal: the bounds set a stride, not a filter

items.item: A clustered, skewed key sends nearly all its rows into whichever single partition's stride covers that clustered range, measured directly: two thousand rows in the first partition, zero in fourteen more, forty-eight thousand in the last.

Increasing the partition count does not proportionally fix a skewed key's imbalance, because the skew lives in the data's own distribution, not in how many pieces the range is cut into — measured directly at sixty-four partitions, where the busiest partition still held over sixteen thousand rows.

A REPEATABLE READ transaction's pg_export_snapshot lets a second, fully separate connection see the exact same data, unaffected by a concurrent commit in between — a fresh connection with no snapshot sees the new row instead.

at.step: Reveal: a consistent snapshot across workers

items.item: COPY TO measured faster than a row-by-row SELECT fetchall over the identical rows, every trial run this session, which is why it is the bulk path to reach for first.

at.step: Reveal: COPY against row-by-row SELECT, measured

items.item: Offloading a long read to a replica does not remove its cost: without hot_standby_feedback the replica's own query risks cancellation; with it, the primary's own cleanup is held back instead, for as long as the replica's query needs.

at.step: Reveal: a replica moves the cost, it does not remove it

items.item: A long-running extract's own open snapshot pins the xmin horizon on the table it reads, exactly like a replica's hot_standby_feedback pins it on the primary — measured directly: ten thousand dead tuples that a real VACUUM run cannot reclaim while that snapshot is still open.

at.step: Reveal: the vacuum cost, measured directly

items.item: VACUUM running does not guarantee cleanup happens; it only reclaims row versions nothing still needs, so a long transaction elsewhere makes a VACUUM run a no-op for the rows it's protecting.

at.step: Reveal: the vacuum cost, measured directly

items.item: The fetchsize option exists specifically because some JDBC drivers default to a very small round-trip batch size (the Spark docs name Oracle's ten-row default as the motivating example), so a default-tuned driver can silently make a large extract far slower than it needs to be.
